title: Hardships of touring: 109 towns, unpaid shows and hunger
summary: Long overnight jumps, a show that could not pay, chorus girls going hungry, and charging postage stamps to the hotel bill.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: I forgot after, because I had left town. I didn't know what happened to him after that, until I saw him at the jazz club, you know? Because I was going for about five years there, one trip. I didn't think I made 109 towns in one year. Gee, I was really jumping. I'd make an overnight jump for 500 miles, and I'd leave out of Jackson, Mississippi, and jump into Jackson, Tennessee, or something like that, you know? I'd play there maybe one night or two nights, and then I was going again. I could jump up to, around Chicago, and we played Gary and Aurora and St. Charles and Jolliette, Chicago, and play around that section there. And then maybe, and then jump, jump then into Minneapolis and play around there, and then get back into South Carolina, North Carolina. Just jumping all the time. Never forget one time there, we started out in Arkansas. Oh man, that was a, you talk about a slow boat to China. It was a slow process getting, getting out of that state. We, we really was on a panic. We were on a, the show wasn't making no money. They had to charge the baggage to the hotel, and leave it there, and go to the next town, and borrow money from the show to send back to the hotel to pick up the props and all the baggage, and move it into the next town. Talking about hardships. So, these chorus gals here that you saw here, they were always hungry, you know. So I'll never forget that. This little band there, we used to travel around a little old model there ford. This guy here was named Fliver Ford. You can see he's got a little tam on, with a banjo play. His name was Fliver Ford. So, we used to travel around this little old model there ford, you know. Get, get in the town in the morning. Man, we'd be hungry, boys. This guy would say, where do we eat? Well, the boss man, he, he, he, what that, and he says, eat? He said, you all look like ducks now. You can't throw your legs up in the morning. You're worried about eating. And, he wouldn't, he wouldn't feed us that morning, man. That was the funny part about it. We were hungry. I'll never forget the time my, my wife said, what's the matter? You don't write no more. I said, well, if you send me some stamps, I'll write you. And we're charging the stamps to the hotel bills. That's right. That's how rough it was, you know. But, uh, off and all, no, we'd have a bad break. You know how it is, man. You'd get a good break. Now, that's, that same show started with a bad break. And we wound up making plenty of money with that show. And all kind of offers. With this Hollywood Scandal show. Every, everybody thought it was from Hollywood, you know. They saw it. And it, man, it made plenty of money when it got on that, Sanger circuit for a while. And we got through there. And, you know, if they're getting out of Arkansas, you know, you play these old, uh, independent houses, you know. And they just depend upon what they can get at night. And they couldn't pay the show off. So they owed you the money. So what could you do? And you had to just struggle and struggle until you hit it good. And, uh, the same as many times I played in the town for room and board and we spotted out at night. Well, we, uh, we, uh, we were sure of one thing to eat. And, uh, sleep. And we'd catch one or two or three spot jobs a week. And we had a little money in our pocket. But sometimes we made big money. Sometimes we didn't. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
